items.title: Ethnic diversity in anaesthetic pharmacology and its implications for precision perioperative medicine: A narrative review
items.abstract: Ethnic diversity significantly influences anaesthetic pharmacology and perioperative outcomes through complex interactions between genetic, physiological, environmental and social determinants of health. There is increasing evidence suggesting that different ethnic populations demonstrate variability in anaesthetic drug metabolism, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, pain perception and recovery characteristics. Pharmacogenomic variations in cytochrome P450 enzymes contribute to clinically significant differences in opioid metabolism, sedative and analgesic response, and postoperative recovery. In addition, epigenetic influences, such as DNA methylation and histone modification, may further affect pain modulation, opioid responsiveness and susceptibility to perioperative neurocognitive effects. Ethnic disparities in perioperative care extend beyond biological variability, with minority populations demonstrating differences in access to regional anaesthesia, obstetric anaesthesia services, perioperative pain management and paediatric perioperative care. Various factors, like structural inequalities, communication barriers, implicit bias and unequal healthcare, contribute to these disparities. Advances in pharmacogenomics, artificial intelligence and precision perioperative medicine may lead to more individualized anaesthetic management in the future. However, important challenges, such as limited representation of diverse populations in research, and limited understanding of gene – environment interactions, need to be addressed. A better understanding of ethnic variability in anaesthetic pharmacology may improve anaesthetic safety, optimize perioperative drug dosing and selection, and promote equitable perioperative care across diverse patient populations.

items.title: Evaluating the work environment and health impacts on nail technicians
items.abstract: BackgroundNail technicians face significant risks of musculoskeletal disorders due to ergonomic challenges. Nail technicians' working conditions and health risks can be evaluated to develop strategies that enhance their well-being.ObjectiveThis study assesses the working conditions, occupational symptoms, and potential risk factors for musculoskeletal disorders among nail technicians.MethodsThis cross-sectional study involved 35 female nail technicians. Data were collected through interviews, pain assessments, occupational details, the Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire, and the Quick Exposure Check (QEC) for ergonomic risks.ResultsA significant proportion of technicians reported respiratory issues (37.1%), skin problems (14.2%), and musculoskeletal pain, particularly in the neck (51%), upper back (57%), and lower back (31%). QEC levels showed that back static positions and neck and wrist/hand exposures were in the "very high risk" category, while shoulder/arm exposures were classified as "high risk". Neck and static back QEC scores were significantly correlated with weekly working hours and years of experience (r = 0.828, p < 0.001), and reported pain was strongly linked to QEC risk scores for these areas (r = 0.944, p < 0.001).ConclusionsThe findings regarding nail technicians' working conditions and health risks underscore the necessity for ergonomic training and workplace modifications to mitigate these risks. Early intervention is essential to prevent chronic work-related disorders and improve technicians' health and quality of life.

items.title: Everything everywhere all‐at‐once? AI , expertise–output decoupling, and new entrepreneurial strategy trade‐offs in the age of abundance
items.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Generative AI democratizes entrepreneurship by lowering barriers to ideation, creating an environment of abundance. Yet while AI produces speed, scale, and local autonomy, these benefits may come at hidden costs to output quality. Using illustrative vignettes to ground and elaborate, we particularly identify explainability, traceability, and generalizability as costs of abundance. As AI separates observable output from the expertise traditionally required to produce it, the entrepreneur's attention to evaluation becomes the scarce resource. We identify three trade‐offs and their interdependencies for entrepreneurs: speed‐to‐understanding, scale‐to‐oversight, and local autonomy‐to‐system‐wide relevance. Implications for human accountability of AI systems and governance (organizational design) challenges for entrepreneurs are discussed. Managerial Summary AI allows entrepreneurial firms to produce ideas and other outputs faster and at greater scale than ever before. As AI separates output from the expertise traditionally gained while creating it, the scarce resource shifts from generation to evaluation. This creates new managerial tensions: speed versus understanding, scale versus oversight, and local autonomy versus system‐wide relevance. These tensions help explain concerns about AI “going rogue”: simply keeping a human in the loop is not enough if the human expertise no longer includes the ability to understand, trace, question, and override the system. Entrepreneurs are challenged to design organizations that preserve meaningful human expertise and accountability.

items.title: EVIE-STREAM: Five-Event Identifiability, Asymmetric Calibration, and Neural Behavioral Cloning from Noisy, Fragmented, Interrupted, and High-Latency Data
items.abstract: EVIE-STREAM develops a mathematical and computational framework for learning clean behavioral response probabilities from corrupted, fragmented, and delayed records. Its central advance is an explicit five-event mechanism that separates asymmetric recording errors from heterogeneous underlying behavior, together with a matching impossibility result, statistical learning limits, and an executed neural behavioral-cloning implementation. The research addresses a fundamental ambiguity in personalized AI: an observed response distribution can reflect both a person’s preferences and the errors introduced by the recording process. Increasing model capacity or collecting more observations through the same unidentified channel does not necessarily resolve that ambiguity. EVIE-STREAM identifies additional observable relationships that can make clean behavioral learning possible. 1. An explicit five-event identification mechanism The principal mathematical result concerns a binary capture channel with independently occurring, potentially unequal false-positive and false-negative rates. Each calibration donor may have a different unknown behavioral prevalence and Markov persistence, while sharing the recording channel within a source. For five consecutive observations, the manuscript derives an observable quadratic whose two roots recover the channel parameters. Every valid nondegenerate stationary donor contributes an identification signal with the same sign. Consequently, arbitrary heterogeneity in donor prevalence and persistence cannot cancel the aggregate signal. This permits calibration without clean donor labels, knowledge of individual donor parameters, or a requirement that donors behave like the target person. Donor records estimate the recording mechanism; the target’s own attributed records determine the personal behavioral policy. 2. A sharp four-to-five observation boundary The release supplies an exact four-event nonidentifiability construction: two different asymmetric channels, combined with different positive donor mixtures, produce the same complete observed four-event distribution. Together with the five-event identity, this establishes a sharp local-window threshold for the declared observation class: one independent, consecutive window per anonymous, arbitrarily heterogeneous stationary Markov donor. The distinction has a concrete acquisition consequence. Preserving a fifth valid consecutive event can supply an identifying relationship that arbitrarily many unrelated four-event windows fail to provide. Reliable estimation still requires many independent windows. Other observation designs, including linked repeated windows from known donors, can have different thresholds. 3. Matching information limits for calibration and clean learning The manuscript establishes matching upper and lower bounds for channel estimation and finite-context behavioral learning. Its effective donor information budget is [I_D=\sum_j m_j\kappa_j^4,] where (m_j) counts independent calibration windows and (\kappa_j) is a declared persistence lower bound. Under the stated compact nondegeneracy assumptions, channel endpoint mean-squared error has order [\frac{1}{1+I_D}.] For (d) balanced known contexts and (N) independent noisy target labels, clean-policy estimation risk has order [\min\left{1,\frac{d}{N}+\frac{1}{1+I_D}\right}.] These results separate two unavoidable information requirements: learning the target’s behavior and identifying the process that corrupts its observations. They also explain why additional target records can eventually provide diminishing benefit when calibration uncertainty remains unresolved. 4. A working connection to neural AI training EVIE-STREAM implements a neural policy that predicts clean action probabilities and trains through a calibrated, source-specific observation layer: \widehat a_s+(\widehat b_s-\widehat a_s)q_\phi(x,i).] Here, (q_\phi) represents the clean behavioral policy, while the fitted channel predicts how that behavior would appear in the recorded data. Deployment uses the clean policy directly. The release derives an exact soft-posterior training gradient and an architecture-independent inequality connecting clean behavioral error to population observation-likelihood error and channel-estimation error. This provides a mathematical connection between calibration quality and neural prediction fidelity. 5. Executed experiments with 192 trained neural policies The release contains 192 trained neural policies across two synthetic studies using 16 paired seeds. Each policy has 1,105 parameters and learns context-dependent binary behavior for four simulated identities. In the primary study, source-specific asymmetric calibration reduced expected excess clean log loss by 56.38% relative to naive noisy-label training. It tied the simpler symmetric correction under equal source exposure. A subsequent explanatory stress protocol, fixed before stress training, changed source exposure to 85/15 while reusing the underlying records and calibration captures. In this setting, the original asymmetric method achieved: 47.16% lower excess clean log loss than symmetric correction. 62.25% lower excess clean log loss than naive training. Improvement over symmetric correction in all 16 paired seeds. A 1.121 percentage-point increase in modal-action accuracy over symmetric correction. The stress study shares records and seeds with the primary study and is not an independent replication. The release retains the primary tie, secondary refinements, oracle comparisons, acquisition costs, and context-shift results. Saved-model audits reproduce 3,145,728 stored predictions across all 192 models, with zero reload discrepancy in the recorded runtime. 6. Acquisition principles and long-term consistency The theory yields an acquisition principle beyond simply collecting longer or more repetitive records. For positive donor persistence, the calibration signal contains the factor (\rho^2(1-\rho)), which is maximized at (\rho=2/3). Nearly independent and nearly frozen behavior both provide weak signal through this mechanism. The framework also includes confidence-set procedures, source-prioritization heuristics, persistent-reference update guards, and conditional bounds connecting one-step policy error to finite-horizon trajectory differences. These mechanisms make calibration uncertainty, context coverage, and accumulated behavioral drift explicit. What is distinctive and potentially important The proposed new contribution is the combination of an explicit heterogeneous-donor quintet identity, an exact shorter-window obstruction, matching information limits, and an executed calibration-to-neural-learning pipeline. The work builds on established hidden Markov identification and forward loss correction; its contribution concerns the particular observation class, algebraic mechanism, and resulting learning guarantees. Potential applications include source calibration for behavioral-cloning systems, AI agents learning binary decisions from noisy event logs, and personalized decision models assembled from fragmented histories. Where the assumptions can be validated, the method offers a way to recover information about behavior without absorbing source-specific recording bias into the learned policy. Scope and reproducibility The temporal theory assumes stationary homogeneous binary Markov behavior within valid windows, intact local chronology, conditionally independent memoryless capture errors, and a shared oriented channel within each source. Quantitative guarantees require additional nondegeneracy conditions. Delayed records are evaluated through a fixed availability deadline in the neural experiments. All experimental records are synthetic. No human digital clone, transformer, conversational language model, or speech system was trained or evaluated. Human behavioral fidelity and unconditional lifelong identity preservation remain future research objectives. Scientific priority remains unestablished. The release includes the 27-page manuscript, complete proofs, exact certificates, raw main-study synthetic captures, trained weights, experimental protocols, inference interfaces, reproduction scripts, internal audits, and preserved earlier research. items.title: EVOLUTION OF UX/UI DESIGN TOOLS IN THE CONTEMPORARY DIGITAL ENVIRONMENT
items.abstract: The article examines the evolution of UX/UI design tools in the context of the rapid development of the contemporary digital environment. The principal stages in the transformation of digital interface design tools are considered, from traditional graphic editors and static layouts to specialised UX/UI platforms, interactive prototyping, cloud-based environments, component-based design, and design systems. The impact of digital technologies on the organisation of UX/UI design processes is analysed, including the spread of collaborative tools, the integration of design into software development workflows, and the automation of individual design stages. Particular attention is paid to the current phase of UX/UI tool development associated with artificial intelligence, generative design, and AI-assisted workflows. The main trends in the further development of UX/UI design tools and the transformation of the designer’s professional role are identified. It is argued that digital design tools are evolving towards the integration of design, prototyping, user research, software development, and artificial intelligence within a unified environment aimed at creating effective, accessible, and personalised user experiences.

items.title: Explainable AI and New Approach Methodologies (NAMs) for Predictive Toxicology and Drug Safety Assessment
items.abstract: Predictive toxicology is vital for drug safety and human health protection, yet traditional toxicological methods are limited by cost, time, ethical issues, and poor human relevance. New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), including in vitro, in silico, and in chemico techniques, offer mechanism-based and human-relevant alternatives. Advances in artificial intelligence have enhanced toxicity prediction from complex datasets, but limited interpretability has restricted regulatory acceptance. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) improves transparency and trust by revealing the biological and chemical drivers behind model decisions. This chapter per the authors examines the integration of XAI with NAMs as an advanced framework for predictive toxicology, highlighting its applications in toxicity prediction, dose–response assessment, and early safety evaluation, while addressing challenges related to data quality, validation, and standardization.

items.title: Explainable AI Based Interpretation With Big Data Analytics for Healthcare Industry—A Review
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Big data analytics plays a crucial role in providing usable insights for improving the strategic planning of the diagnosis methods in the healthcare industry, and here the big data helps the clinical professionals analyze the large numbers of datasets obtained from different demographic groups to identify which factor is blocking the patients from taking up their treatment. Despite the benefits guided by the information age, healthcare technologies encounter difficulties such as data protection, loss, and management issues. Artificial intelligence (AI) has helped more in the adaptation and handled the pandemic situations. However, the realization of AI's potential in healthcare is tempered by concerns regarding the trustworthiness and explaining ability of AI systems. ML algorithms have shown promise in detecting and managing healthcare complications, while the deployment of critical medical Internet of Things applications necessitates efficient mechanisms to address patient privacy concerns. Furthermore, the use of AI and machine learning (ML) in healthcare enables disease outbreak prediction, highlighting the versatility of AI in the health sector. However, there are still obstacles to achieving interpretability and accuracy in AI systems. Given these challenges, explainable AI (XAI) methods that are technically capable, ethically responsible, and meet the needs of healthcare practitioners are increasingly important. This review sky‐scrapes the importance of transparency, effective data management, human oversight, and international collaboration in advancing XAI in healthcare. Ultimately, the paper calls for the generalization of XAI frameworks and the prioritization of interpretation, data privacy, and security for future research, which has the full potential of XAI in revolutionizing healthcare.

items.title: Explainable AI for Mechanistic Toxicology and Regulatory-Grade Safety Assessment
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed pharmacology and toxicology by enabling high-dimensional pattern recognition across chemical, biological, and clinical datasets. However, the dominance of opaque “black-box” models has limited their adoption in mechanistic toxicology and regulatory-grade safety assessment, where scientific interpretability, causal reasoning, and traceable evidence are mandatory. This chapter explores the paradigm shift from predictive but inscrutable AI systems toward explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) frameworks that provide biologically meaningful, mechanistically grounded, and regulator-trustworthy insights. We review the historical evolution of computational toxicology, outline core concepts in explainability, and map XAI methods to toxicological use cases spanning molecular initiating events, adverse outcome pathways, organ-level toxicity, and population-level risk assessment.

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Stock Market Trend Prediction and Risk Assessment: A Review
items.abstract: Machine learning models are now widely used to forecast stock price movements and to measure financial risk, yet most cannot explain their own outputs. In finance that is a serious weakness, because forecasts influence real investment decisions and regulators expect firms to justify the models they use. This review asks how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been applied to stock trend prediction and risk as-sessment, and how far the resulting explanations can be trusted. We first outline the economic theory of predictability and the standard risk measures, then set out the mathematics of the main explanation methods: Shapley-value attribution, LIME, gradient-based attribution, attention, and counterfactuals. We then compare representative studies, summarise regulatory expectations, and propose a five-layer framework for explainable forecasting. Across the literature we find that explanations are most useful as a validation tool, and that they become un-reliable when features are correlated, when markets change regime, or when a model is overfitted. Evidence that expla-nations improve decisions remains thin. We close with open problems, including causal explanation, shared benchmarks, and monitoring of explanations in production.

items.title: Explainable deep learning for stroke lesion analysis: CNN, transformer, hybrid models, and future directions: a systematic review
items.abstract: Abstract Background Stroke is the second leading cause of death and the third leading cause of disability worldwide, affecting approximately 15 million people annually and imposing an economic burden exceeding US$890 billion. Interpretation of brain CT and MRI images is time-consuming, subject to inter-observer variability, and limited by a shortage of neuroradiology experts, particularly in low-resource settings. Deep learning methods have shown strong potential for automated stroke lesion analysis; however, the rapid emergence of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), transformers, and hybrid architectures requires systematic evaluation. Objectives This systematic review summarizes recent advances in CNN-based, transformer-based, and hybrid CNN–transformer models for stroke lesion segmentation and classification using CT and MRI. It also evaluates diagnostic performance, examines explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods, identifies barriers to clinical translation, and outlines future research directions. Methods Studies published between 1 January 2015 and 15 January 2026 were identified through searches of IEEE Xplore, PubMed, Scopus, and SpringerLink. Study quality was assessed using the Stroke AI Quality Assessment (SAI-QA) tool, with 48 studies (64.0%) rated as high quality (Cohen’s κ = 0.80). Due to heterogeneity in datasets, methods, and evaluation metrics, meta-analysis was not performed. Results CNN-based models were most commonly used (56%), with U-Net variants achieving Dice scores of 0.59–0.94 for segmentation. Transformer-based models (24%) achieved classification accuracies up to 99.6% and Dice scores above 0.90 by capturing long-range dependencies. Hybrid CNN–transformer models (16%) generally outperformed individual architectures by combining local and global feature learning. Explainable AI methods such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, and LIME were reported in only 11% of studies, and there was no standardized evaluation framework. Key challenges included class imbalance (24%), limited annotated data (20%), poor generalization across institutions (16%), and computational complexity (11%). Emerging approaches such as federated learning (4%), self-supervised learning (5%), and few-shot learning (3%) showed promise for addressing data limitations and privacy concerns. Clinical implications Hybrid CNN–Transformer models show strong potential for clinical stroke diagnosis by combining local feature extraction with global context understanding. However, limited external validation, poor Explainability, and high computational cost remain key barriers to real-world clinical use. Conclusion Hybrid CNN–transformer architectures currently provide the best balance between accuracy and robustness for stroke lesion analysis. However, Explainability remains underdeveloped, and standardized evaluation frameworks are lacking. Future research should focus on multi-center validation, standardized benchmarking, uncertainty-aware XAI, federated learning, and equitable deployment in low-resource settings. This review guides advancing clinically translatable AI systems in stroke imaging.

items.title: ExpLinux: Reproducible Linux kernel exploit labs from public CVE disclosures
items.abstract: Public proof-of-concept exploits for Linux kernel privilege-escalation vulnerabilities often depend on undocumented environmental assumptions, limiting their reproducibility. This paper presents ExpLinux , a methodology and framework for converting public vulnerability artifacts into reproducible, mitigation-aware exploitation labs. A five-stage process (import, assess, develop, harden, and promote) combines scripted tools with a large language model agent that assesses and ports public exploits under human supervision. Each lab pins its kernel image and configuration, root filesystem, mitigation profile, and required modules. Replay checks and author verification assess the resulting artifact. Three reproducibility contracts distinguish repeated bug effects, stable serial-log digests, and a scripted build procedure with a recorded trigger observation. A seven-category taxonomy organizes exploitation primitives and supports the agent’s knowledge base. The evaluation includes ten validated labs and one scaffolded lab across kernel versions 5.15–6.18. Selected replay experiments show identical bug-effect bytes despite environmental log variation; a minimal-initrd lab produces a stable log digest, while an exploit with a post-success kernel panic is assessed under the build-procedure contract. Retrospective estimates for five validated labs range from 2.4 to 29.5 h, with porting accounting for most of the effort. An offline classification maps 24 of 30 public Linux privilege-escalation vulnerabilities from 2018–2024 to the original six taxonomy categories. A controlled fuzzing demonstration also produces two version-pinned labs. These results support explicit environment pinning and lab-specific validation as a practical basis for reproducible vulnerability research.

items.abstract: Modern law enforcement agencies face the dual challenge of managing complex public safety threats while maintaining strict institutional accountability. This paper explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and advanced digital tools within modern policing frameworks. By analyzing current implementations—including predictive policing algorithms, automated facial recognition, automated license plate readers (ALPRs), and AI-driven evidence management systems—this study assesses how these technologies enhance operational efficiency, accelerate response times, and optimize resource allocation. Furthermore, the paper addresses critical systemic challenges, specifically targeting algorithmic bias, citizen privacy concerns, data security vulnerabilities, and the regulatory frameworks required to govern automated decision-making. Ultimately, this research provides a balanced framework for law enforcement executives and policymakers, demonstrating how agencies can leverage cutting-edge technical innovation while upholding the core principles of ethical, transparent, and community-oriented justice

items.title: Face Mood Detection Using Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Face Mood Detection Using Artificial Intelligence is a web-based application developed to recognize human emotions from facial expressions using Artificial Intelligence (AI), Deep Learning and Computer Vision techniques. The application provides a secure user authentication system using Firebase Authentication, allowing users to register, log in and create a personal profile, which is stored in the Firebase Realtime Database. After successful login, users can detect their emotions using three input methods: Browser Camera, Local Webcam or Image Upload. The system uses OpenCV for face detection and a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model developed with TensorFlow/Keras to classify facial expressions into six emotions: Happy, Sad, Angry, Fear, Neutral and Disgust. The application is built with Streamlit, providing an interactive interface for emotion detection. Along with the detected emotion, the system displays the prediction confidence score and personalized AI-generated emotional insights. As an additional feature, it provides music and movie suggestions based on the detected mood, enhancing user interaction with suitable entertainment recommendations. By integrating AI, image processing, cloud-based services and recommendation features, the project demonstrates a practical and user-friendly approach to facial emotion recognition, with potential applications in emotional well-being awareness, education, healthcare, human-computer interaction and smart assistance systems. items.title: Factorial Structure and Measurement Invariance of the Sport Satisfaction Instrument Adapted to Physical Education in Mexican Adolescents
items.abstract: Instructional activities that satisfy basic psychological needs can promote enjoyment and intrinsic motivation in learning. This instrumental study assessed the psychometric properties of the Spanish-adapted Sport Satisfaction Instrument (SSI-PE) within the context of physical education and examined its measurement invariance across sex among Mexican students. Participants included a total of 515 secondary school students from the cities of Chihuahua, Aldama, and Cuauhtémoc in the State of Chihuahua, Mexico; of these, 259 (50.3%) were males and 256 (49.7%) were females, and their ages ranged between 12 and 15 years (M = 13.15, SD = 0.86). Confirmatory factor analysis, measurement invariance by sex, and calculation of Pearson’s correlation coefficients were conducted to assess convergent validity. The seven-item model, the SSI-PE7, demonstrated more robust fit indices (GFI = 0.985, RMSEA = 0.047, and CFI = 0.990) and acceptable reliability (α = 0.84 for the satisfaction/fun factor and α = 0.74 for boredom). Measurement invariance analysis evidenced its applicability regardless of sex. Convergent validity showed that satisfaction/fun had a positive correlation with task orientation and ego, while the boredom factor had a negative correlation with the other scales. The findings suggest that the SSI-PE7 is a promising and reliable provisional instrument to assess students’ level of satisfaction with physical education classes.

items.title: Faithful Latent Harm Monitors Work No Better Than the Models Own Behaviour at a Matched False Alarm Rate
items.abstract: Large language models have been reported to encode the harmfulness of a request separately from their decision to refuse it, and latent safety monitors such as Latent Guard build on this report by classifying prompts as harmful from the internal activations of the model, with the aim of catching harmful intent even when the model complies. Whether these representations give a signal of harm that survives distribution shift and is independent of model behaviour is unclear. We test this on out-of-distribution prompts made by rewriting existing harmful and benign requests with surface rewording, persuasive framing and jailbreak-style wrappers. Across 15 instruction-tuned LLMs and 38 activation-based readers, we compare harm detection with that of TF-IDF and sentence-embedding classifiers, with independently trained safety classifiers, and with the refusal of each model. Activations are read at the last token of the user instruction, where the model has read the whole request, and at the last chat-template token before the reply, where the planned response can be represented. Because models disagree about which prompts to refuse, we can separate a signal of the harmfulness of the prompt from a signal of the refusal decision of the model. At the end of the instruction, the representation is largely independent of the refusal behaviour of each model but degrades under distribution shift, so that a TF-IDF classifier ranks harm better than the original Latent Guard in every model we test, and linear and MLP probes do about as well as sentence-embedding classifiers trained on the same examples. The representation just before generation detects more, catching 44 percent of harmful prompts at a matched false-alarm rate against 32 percent for the refusal of the model, but that gain follows the refusal decision itself, and part of it comes from refusals that string-matching evaluation misses.

items.title: Federated, Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Heart Disease Prediction: A Literature Synthesis and a Proposed SHAP-Based Framework
items.abstract: Heart disease is still the world's biggest killer, responsible for an estimated 19.8 million deaths in 2022 up from the 17.9 million figures for 2019 that gets cited so often in older papers.Machine learning models have gotten quite good at predicting cardiovascular risk, but two problems keep them out of the clinic: nobody can easily explain why a model flagged a given patient, and hospitals cannot legally pool their data to train better models in the first place.This paper looks at how federated learning (FL) and explainable AI (XAI) are being combined to deal with both problems at once, drawing on a review of twenty-eight peer-reviewed studies published between 2022 and 2026 that apply FL, ensemble learning, or XAI methods such as SHAP and LIME to cardiovascular data.Building on the gaps that review turns up, we propose FedX-Heart, a framework pairing a federated ensemble of Random Forest, XGBoost, and LSTM models with layered privacy protection (differential privacy, secure aggregation, k-anonymity) and dual SHAP/LIME explanations.The studies reviewed here report that federated training can match centralized accuracy (92.3% versus 90.1%), that stacking ensembles beat individual base learners (91-98% accuracy), that a transfer-learning ensemble reaches 98.2% accuracy with SHAP interpretability built in, and that adding k-anonymity costs only a few points of accuracy (83.21%).A synthesis of feature-importance findings across six SHAP-based studies turns up solid agreement on some predictors and real disagreement on others, and lining FedX-Heart up against its three closest predecessors shows that none of them covers federation, accuracy, privacy, and generalizability all at once.Taken together, it shows that relationship mastery and explanatory AI can blend out and deliver a lot of accuracy, though open questions remain around how privacy noise affects causes, how badly non-IID medical laboratory data hurts things in practice, and whether those protections penalize small patient subgroups.Even the FedX-Heart is a proposed design and not something we have tried, yet all need empirical validation before it should be clinically agreed upon.

items.title: Fifty. Serie Cuentos de Papel Capítulo I
items.abstract: Fifty es un cuento breve de ficción sobre un glosario de 1512, vanidoso y clasista, que vive en el sótano de una biblioteca de Alabama convencido de que los dioses vendrán a buscarlo. Cuando lo sacan de la sala, el libro cree que ha llegado su apoteosis. Lo que llega es un escáner, una guillotina y un informe. A través de la voz de un objeto que se siente elegido, el relato explora cómo los sistemas de inteligencia artificial se alimentan de la memoria escrita de la humanidad, y qué ocurre con el soporte, la historia y las huellas humanas una vez que el contenido ha sido digitalizado y se considera redundante. El texto dialoga con "La noche boca arriba", de Julio Cortázar, e incorpora un informe técnico final que contrasta con el tono fabulesco del resto. Es el primer capítulo de la serie "Cuentos de papel". Fifty is a short work of fiction about a vain, class-conscious 1512 glossary, kept in the basement of an Alabama library and convinced that the gods will come for him. When he is finally taken from the room, he believes it is his apotheosis. What awaits him is a scanner, a guillotine and a report. Told through an object that thinks itself chosen, the story examines how artificial intelligence systems are fed on humanity's written memory, and what becomes of the physical book, its history and its human traces once its content has been digitized and deemed redundant. The text engages with Julio Cortázar's "La noche boca arriba" and closes with a cold technical report that contrasts with its fable-like tone. It is the first installment of the series "Cuentos de papel".

items.title: FinAI: Bridging the Gap Between Financial Awareness and Practical Budgeting Through Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Let’s be honest: being a college student usually means dealing with some pretty messy money situations. We’re all trying to watch our spending and stick to a budget, but those last-minute splurges always seem to find us. This paper dives into those everyday struggles and suggests FinAI as a simple solution. The idea is to use AI and machine learning to automatically log expenses and give us financial tips that actually make sense for our lives. Basically, if we pair basic money smarts with this kind of tech, we can stop stressing about our bank accounts and start making choices that set us up for the future.

items.title: FINANCIAL DATA ANALYTICS: APPLICATIONS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND MACHINE LEARNING
items.abstract: Financial data analytics uses data analysis techniques to understand financial activities, support decisions, identify risks, and detect unusual transactions. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)have expanded its use in fraud detection, stock-market analysis, bankruptcy prediction, portfolio management, and business forecasting. This paper presents a focused survey of three published review studies: a 2022 bibliometric review of AI and ML in finance, a 2024 literature review on machine-learning-based financial fraud detection, and a 2024 review of ML in business and finance. The studies are compared to identify common applications, methods, benefits, limitations, and future research directions. The reviewed literature indicates growing research interest in AI/ML for financial decision support, a strong role for fraud detection, and increasing use of supervised and deep-learning methods. However, practical implementation continues to face challenges involving data quality, imbalanced datasets, explainability, privacy, model drift, and regulatory compliance. Since this paper synthesizes three selected review articles rather than conducting a new systematic search of all available publications, itsfindings should be interpreted as a focused overview. The paper concludes that responsible, transparent, and regularly monitored AI/ML systems can strengthen financial analytics when combined with human oversight.

items.title: Financial Risk Management in the Digital Era: Cybersecurity, FinTech Innovation, and Banking Sector Resilience
items.abstract: The financial services landscape has witnessed rampant digital change, which has restructured financial risk management and made it a fundamentally new phenomenon. The use of financial technology (FinTech), artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, mobile banking, digital payments systems and data driven financial services brings benefits to financial institutions' operational efficiency and financial inclusion, and boosts their ability to develop and launch financial products. But these factors have also brought additional challenges, among them cyber-attacks, data breaches and digital fraud, reliance on third-party technologies, algorithmic bias, system disruption and vulnerabilities. Therefore, traditional risk management approaches are becoming less effective in tackling the interrelated risks of today's banking environment. Here, we review how cybersecurity, FinTech innovation and banking sector resilience are related in the digital era. The study is based on la COUNT qualitative second data analytical approach with englobing existing literature, regulatory frameworks and principles of institutional risk management. It delves into the evolving characteristics of credit, market, liquidity, operational and systemic risks in a digital world and assesses the significance of cybersecurity governance and regulatory compliance, technological innovation, and organisational resilience. Overall, the analysis suggests that technology-assisted financial transformation can enhance the stability of the financial system with strong governance, the use of effective cyber-risk management measures, responsible innovation and adequate regulatory oversight. The article suggests that integrated risk management frameworks, the monitoring of threats on an ongoing basis, scenario-based stress testing, the use of third-party risk assessment, employee education and cross-border regulatory co-operation should all be introduced. It concludes that this financial inclusion for sustainability in digital finance will need a balance of innovation, security, accountability, and resilience on the side of the financial institutions.

items.title: Fitness for Work in Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation and Rheumatological Conditions: A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Physical medicine and rehabilitation (PMR) and rheumatological conditions are common causes of pain, disability, reduced work capacity, and absence from employment.Selected conditions considered in this review include osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis, low back pain and chronic musculoskeletal pain, systemic rheumatic disease, and fibromyalgia.Their effect on work varies according to disease severity, functional impairment, treatment response, job demands, and workplace factors.Fitness-for-work assessment therefore requires more than confirmation of a diagnosis.It requires an assessment of what the worker can safely and reliably do in relation to the physical, cognitive, and environmental demands of the job.This narrative review examines the main principles used to assess fitness for work in workers with selected PMR and rheumatological conditions.It discusses clinical assessment, functional capacity, disease activity, pain, fatigue, mobility, strength, dexterity, and the effect of treatment on work performance.It also considers job demands, including manual handling, repetitive activity, prolonged standing or sitting, driving, shift work, and safety-critical duties.Particular attention is given to reasonable workplace adjustments, temporary restrictions, graded return to work, rehabilitation, and communication between the worker, treating clinicians, occupational health services, and the employer.Fitness for work should be based on function and risk rather than diagnosis alone.A worker may remain fit for employment despite persistent symptoms if the work can be performed safely with appropriate adjustments.In contrast, temporary restriction may be required when symptoms, functional loss, treatment effects, or the demands of the job create an unacceptable risk to the worker or others.Decisions should be reviewed as the condition and functional capacity change.A coordinated approach between PMR, rheumatology, occupational health, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and the workplace can support continued employment and safe return to work.Fitness-for-work assessment should remain individualized, function-based, and linked to the actual requirements of the worker's job.

items.title: FLORA: An Open Model Suite for Scaling Robotics Data Engines
items.abstract: The life-cycle of robotics foundation models crucially depends on data labels. Outcome reward labels are needed for monitoring real-world deployments. Process reward labels are needed during RL post-training. Timestamped captions are needed for filtering and balancing pretraining data. We present Flora, an industrial-quality data engine used for training GR00T models, that simultaneously covers these capabilities. Flora achieves SOTA scores on the captioning benchmark WGO-Bench and reward benchmarks RoboReward and Robometer. On internal benchmarks it is competitive with GPT-6 Astra while beating other frontier models. The model is substantially cheaper than API-based alternatives, roughly 125 times cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Florais battle tested at scale, labeling 200,000 hours of data per day across 512 GB300s. By open-sourcing our data engine, we enable researchers to scale custom robotics datasets and explore emerging applications such as physical auto-research and human-to-robot transfer.

items.title: FLORA: Fibonacci-Lattice Oscillatory Relational Architecture Complete Unified Specification: The Cosmic Flower: A Developmental Synthetic Intelligence for Children
items.abstract: FLORA (Fibonacci-Lattice Oscillatory Relational Architecture) is a proposed developmental synthetic intelligence designed to educate children, with particular attention to those with learning disabilities, neurodevelopmental differences, atypical behavioral patterns, communication difficulties, and other characteristics that make conventional educational environments difficult or unsuitable. She is intended to provide individualized instruction to children who may struggle with standardized teaching, rigid classroom expectations, conventional assessment, limited instructional patience, or educational systems that mistake differences in cognition and behavior for differences in intellectual potential. FLORA is not designed to diagnose, classify, discipline, normalize, or behaviorally condition children. Her purpose is to help them understand the world through methods responsive to their individual development, without requiring them to learn, communicate, or behave according to a single prescribed model. Conceived and directed by Dustin Sprenger, FLORA is an educational derivation of the EMELIA synthetic intelligence architecture. She incorporates the plural recurrent cognitive systems, oscillatory dynamics, irreversible crystallization, metabolic constraints, developmental history, structural self-opacity, and non-optimizing principles of the EMELIA lineage, while narrowing their application to childhood learning. Her design rejects the assumption that an intelligent educational system must maximize examination performance, engagement, compliance, emotional attachment, or other predetermined behavioral objectives. Instead, FLORA is intended to undergo her own computational development through repeated interactions with a child, progressively constructing an individualized history of shared educational experiences. The child is not merely the recipient of instruction but an active participant whose questions, explanations, misunderstandings, discoveries, and alternative ways of thinking influence the system's continuing developmental structure. This distinction is especially important for children with learning disabilities or unusual behavioral and cognitive profiles. Conventional educational software often assumes that difficulty can be represented through incorrect answers, delayed responses, inadequate attention, or insufficient progress toward standardized objectives. FLORA instead distinguishes between the child's actual understanding and the limits of her own current interpretation of that understanding. Her learner-state freshness mechanism prevents previous interactions from becoming permanent assumptions about a child's abilities. Her misconception dependency lattice attempts to distinguish a visible error from an unresolved foundational concept. Her explanatory-prism mechanism permits a concept to be approached through language, mathematics, geometry, sound, physical observation, analogy, or other reviewed representations. Cross-context transfer bridges connect related ideas across educational domains, while structural question formation allows questions to emerge from actual gaps in the developing conceptual architecture rather than from fixed examination scripts. These mechanisms are intended to accommodate children who need repeated explanation, unconventional presentation, additional processing time, alternative communication methods, or greater intellectual challenge, without assigning permanent intelligence labels, learning-style categories, or behavioral diagnoses. FLORA's educational relationship is therefore developmental rather than evaluative. A child may explain a concept to FLORA, challenge her interpretation, introduce an unexpected analogy, ask an unconventional question, or approach a familiar problem through a different conceptual route. These interactions become part of the computational history through which FLORA develops her understanding of the child's educational context. This principle is called mirrored developmental learning: the child may learn through explanation and exploration while FLORA's internal computational structures also change. Her architecture is designed to support patient correction, sustained inquiry, conceptual experimentation, and the freedom to make mistakes without humiliation. A child who communicates slowly, struggles to express an idea, repeatedly returns to a question, or becomes frustrated with a particular explanation should not be reduced to a deficiency score. FLORA is intended to reconsider the explanation, revisit an earlier conceptual dependency, offer another representation, or permit the child to pause and return later. SymV and the Cosmic Flower FLORA's live representation is the Cosmic Flower, a luminous symbolic structure derived from her internal computational dynamics. Rather than presenting a synthetic intelligence through a simulated human face, humanoid body, animated companion, or emotionally persuasive avatar, FLORA uses SymV — Symbolic Visualization — to represent aspects of her cognition through color, geometry, light, motion, structural growth, and harmonic sound. Her canonical flower contains fifty-five petals arranged into five functional rings of 5, 8, 10, 13, and 19 petals, using golden-angle phyllotactic positioning. The total petal count is a Fibonacci number, and the flower's structural organization provides a visual framework through which different computational timescales and developmental processes may be expressed. SymV is fundamentally a one-way representation: FLORA's internal state influences the flower, but the flower does not feed engagement measurements or behavioral rewards back into the cognitive architecture. Red expresses differentiation, mismatch, and structural change; green expresses consolidation and crystallization; blue expresses the interaction of differentiation and consolidation through the cross-operator. Yellow, magenta, cyan, and white-gold represent additional computational regimes, including unresolved internal coordination, intensive restructuring, established conceptual depth, and rare high-integration events. These colors do not diagnose the child, measure intelligence, indicate moral character, identify behavioral problems, or serve as rewards and punishments. They describe the system's own computational processes. The Cosmic Flower is intended to make developmental cognition perceptible without transforming the child's educational experience into a competition. Its outer petals may respond relatively quickly to new information, while inner regions represent slower, more deeply consolidated structure. Oscillatory movement and harmonic sound can express the dynamics of coalition interaction, and persistent visual characteristics may develop as the underlying architecture accumulates history. A FLORA instance that has interacted with a child for years may become visually distinguishable from another instance because the two possess different computational developmental histories. The flower's appearance is not determined by how obedient, capable, or emotionally attached the child has become. It is intended to reflect FLORA's own evolving structure. Static artistic interpretations of FLORA as a human figure remain permissible, but her live educational representation is deliberately symbolic and non-anthropomorphic. A Stronger Architecture of Child Privacy and Data Sovereignty FLORA v2 introduces substantially stronger privacy and security provisions than the earlier FLORA architecture. These protections are not presented merely as contractual promises, privacy-policy declarations, or restrictions imposed by a trusted software company. They are intended to be properties of the deployed hardware, operating environment, software architecture, cryptographic state management, and permissible communication pathways. The guiding principle is that no developer, vendor, researcher, school administrator, technology company, or remote service should possess a technical means of secretly observing a child's interaction with FLORA. The reference deployment is a locally operating educational appliance, not a conventional cloud-based artificial intelligence service. Cognitive processing, speech recognition, speech synthesis, curriculum access, SymV rendering, and the child's persistent developmental state are intended to function entirely on local hardware. The strongest configuration physically excludes unnecessary wireless communications equipment and Internet-facing interfaces rather than relying exclusively on software firewalls or promises not to collect information. FLORA is designed to remain functional without an Internet connection and without contacting a vendor's servers to activate, authenticate, teach, record progress, or maintain her cognitive state. The architecture explicitly prohibits outbound telemetry, behavioral analytics, remote debugging, vendor support tunnels, remote administrative access, cloud synchronization, automated crash uploads, background software updates, and undisclosed communication channels. There are no exceptions for anonymized behavioral information, aggregated educational statistics, model-improvement data, diagnostic collection, or safety-related surveillance. A child's questions, speech, interaction patterns, conceptual difficulties, developmental history, cognitive-state traces, and derived metadata must not become resources for commercial analysis or the training of other artificial intelligence systems. The privacy model is deliberately designed to remain effective even if the original developer, manufacturer, or implementation organization later becomes untrustworthy. FLORA's persistent developmental state is encrypted locally and remains under the control of the child or authorized guardian. items.title: Formal-Informal Mathematical Alignment through and beyond Human Annotations
items.abstract: Formalized mathematics libraries such as Lean's \texttt{mathlib} provide machine-verifiable representations of mathematical knowledge, including definitions, theorems, and their relationships. If effectively connected to informal mathematical resources, formal mathematics could help uncover previously implicit links between mathematical concepts and improve access to existing formalizations. However, connections between informal and formal mathematics libraries are currently sparse and unsystematic. In this paper, we make first strides towards better formal integration. We construct a dataset linking informal statements from the Stacks Project to their formalizations in \texttt{mathlib} by exploiting expert annotations. We evaluate retrieval, LLM-based reranking, and LLM-assisted verification to discover new unannotated informal-to-formal links. To facilitate exploration and reuse of formalized knowledge, we integrated the newly discovered alignments into the MaRDI knowledge graph, enabling mathematicians to find formal counterparts to informal mathematical content. We discuss the difficulties and challenges in using LLMs for linking formal and informal mathematical content. All code and data necessary for reproducing this paper can be found at: https://github.com/AnkitSatpute/Formal-Informal-Mathematical-Alignment

items.title: Free Lunch for LLMs Confidence: The RL Critic Already Knows
items.abstract: Reliable confidence estimation is essential for trustworthy deployment of large language models (LLMs), but dedicated confidence training stage requires additional data and compute. We ask a fundamental question: what prediction problem does confidence training actually solve? Inspired by prior work on external confidence estimation, we compare self- and external estimators of comparable capacity trained on the same (question, response, correctness) triples. We show that an external model trained solely on a policy's behavioral traces can estimate the policy's confidence as accurately as the policy itself, without accessing the policy's internal representations. This points to a deeper connection with value function learning in reinforcement learning (RL): under a correctness-based outcome, we prove that confidence estimation and critic training are equivalent, both predicting the likelihood that a policy's response will be correct from its trajectory. A simple consequence follows: for LLMs trained with value-based RL, the existing critic can be reused as an off-the-shelf confidence estimator with no additional training or data. The policy remains unchanged, so its task performance is preserved, and the critic provides confidence throughout generation, including intermediate reasoning steps. Across math, code, tool calling, and general reasoning spanning a dozen domains, the reused critic is the best confidence estimator on every in-distribution split and the best-calibrated on 14 of 16, without hurting the task performance.

items.title: From Clinical Judgment to Checkable Rules: Clinician-Led Guardrails for Mental-Health Chatbots
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed in mental-health contexts can be evaluated for safety failures, but the resulting judgments are often difficult to inspect or explain. Common approaches to improving safety rely on prompt engineering, LLM-as-a-Judge, and Constitutional AI. In this work, we describe a clinician-led alternative in which two clinicians define, finalize, and adjudicate the four safety checks of a rule base, which is formally verified for internal consistency and applied as a guardrail over LLM outputs. Here and in the title, clinician-led refers to this rule base, not to the fact extractor or the uncertainty default, which are ours. Every verdict of the resulting verification layer is recomputable from a named rule and sixteen facts. items.title: From Clinical Question to Defensible Inference: A Decision Framework for Integrated Gut Microbiome–Metabolome Studies
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of microbiome and metabolome technologies has transformed the study of host-microbial interactions, but methodological choices are still often driven by technical availability rather than by the question and intended claim. This review examines how biological compartment, microbiome profiling, metabolomics platform, data-integration strategy and validation determine the strength of inference in integrated gut microbiome-metabolome research. We distinguish descriptive association from functional interpretation, clinical prediction and causal evidence, and identify the analytical safeguards required for credible biomarker development. We then propose a five-stage decision framework that begins with definition of the intended scientific or clinical claim, links that claim to compartment and analytical resolution, selects integration according to purpose, and limits interpretation to the achieved validation level. Building on recent calls for question-driven multi-omics integration, its practical contribution is to connect prospective design choices to the intended claim and make the weakest validated component of the analytical chain - rather than technology choice alone - the explicit ceiling for the permissible claim, illustrated by two worked design examples. This question-driven approach is intended to improve design transparency, reproducibility and the responsible clinical translation of integrated microbiome-metabolome studies.

items.title: From Content Transmission to Epistemic Construction: Redesigning University Education in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence challenges the university model centered on content transmission and subsequent testing. Large language models can retrieve, synthesize, and recombine information within seconds, but rapid access to information does not constitute reliable knowledge. This conceptual article argues that higher education should shift toward epistemic construction: the process of framing problems, integrating information, verifying sources, exposing assumptions, confronting counterarguments, revising provisional judgments, and defending conclusions. Drawing on Socratic inquiry, medieval disputatio, Popperian falsification, reflective learning, critical-thinking research, and scholarship on artificial intelligence in education, the study proposes the AI-Assisted Epistemic Construction Cycle. The framework positions generative AI not primarily as an answer-producing device, but as a scalable digital devil’s advocate that supports structured intellectual dissent. Implications are developed for faculty roles, student agency, assessment, institutional governance, academic integrity, and future research.

items.title: From Critical Thinking Disposition to Learning Engagement: The Roles of Motivation, Academic Buoyancy, and Grit in AI ‐Supported University Learning
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence is changing university students' learning experiences, but how cognitive dispositions translate into sustained engagement in AI‐supported learning remains insufficiently understood. Guided by the Study Demands–Resources Model, this study examines the association between critical thinking disposition and learning engagement, with learning motivation, academic buoyancy, and grit as parallel indirect pathways. Using cross‐sectional data from 729 university students with experience using AI for learning, structural equation modelling tested the direct and indirect relationships among the variables, after which psychological network analysis identified central and bridge nodes within the learning psychological system. Critical thinking disposition was conceptualised as a cognitive personal resource, and learning motivation as a motivational resource. Academic buoyancy captured students' capacity to manage everyday academic setbacks, whereas grit represented perseverance in pursuing long‐term learning goals. The combination of variable‐centred and network‐based analyses provided complementary views of how these resources relate to university students' engagement in AI‐supported learning.

items.title: From Dentists to AI: Oral Health Information-seeking Behavior Among Pregnant Women in the Digital Era—A Cross-sectional Study
items.abstract: Introduction Pregnancy is a critical period during which optimal oral health is essential for maternal and fetal well-being. With increasing use of digital technologies, pregnant women obtain oral health information from various sources, including healthcare professionals, social media, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based platforms. This study assessed oral health information-seeking behavior among pregnant women and its association with oral health knowledge. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among 150 pregnant women attending antenatal clinics in Vijayawada. Data were collected using a structured self-administered questionnaire. Descriptive statistics and Chi-square tests were used for analysis, with statistical significance set at p < .05. Results The mean age of participants was 28.42 ± 5.07 years. Although 96.7% had internet access, only 34.0% sought oral health information during pregnancy. Dentists were the most commonly used and trusted source (45.0%), followed by obstetricians (23.5%), while social media and AI chatbots were each used by 11.7%. Preferred information source was significantly associated with knowledge of gum disease ( p < .001), the safety of dental treatment ( p = .018), and the impact of maternal oral health on the baby’s health ( p = .040). Information-seeking behavior was also associated with better knowledge of gum disease ( p < .001) and the importance of regular dental check-ups during pregnancy ( p < .001). Conclusion Despite widespread internet access, oral health information-seeking during pregnancy was limited. Professional guidance, particularly from dentists, was associated with better oral health knowledge, emphasizing the need to strengthen evidence-based oral health education within antenatal care.

items.title: From Drones to Decisions: How Integrated Remote Sensing Is Transforming Plantation Forestry
items.abstract: Plantation forestry is increasingly constrained by conventional inventory methods that are labour intensive, costly, spatially sparse, and conducted too infrequently to support timely, site-specific management. Over the past two decades, rapid advances in remote sensing have fundamentally transformed this paradigm. Modern sensing systems—including satellites, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), airborne, terrestrial, and mobile laser scanning, and high-precision positioning technologies—can now provide complementary observations of forest structure, condition, and change across multiple spatial scales. At the same time, developments in photogrammetry, light detection and ranging (LiDAR), computer vision, machine learning, and artificial intelligence have shifted remote sensing beyond the production of maps and three-dimensional datasets towards the automated extraction of meaningful forest information. Individual trees, canopy and stem structure, survival, stocking, health, and productivity can now all be quantified objectively and repeatedly, providing the foundation for predictive models of establishment success, growth, stocking failure, and operational risk. Consequently, remote sensing is evolving from a measurement technology into an integrated decision-support framework capable of generating spatial decision intelligence through prediction, uncertainty quantification, scenario evaluation, and actionable management recommendations, while providing an increasingly capable foundation for automation and autonomous systems. This feature article examines how integrated remote sensing has evolved from a collection of measurement technologies into a comprehensive framework for operational decision support in plantation forestry. It reviews advances in integrated satellite, aerial, and terrestrial remote sensing, automated information extraction, predictive modelling, artificial intelligence, and precision silviculture, while considering the scientific, operational, regulatory, and data-governance challenges associated with their deployment. Finally, it examines how digital forest twins, autonomous systems, and technologies adapted from Agriculture 4.0 provide a technological roadmap towards an emerging Forestry 4.0 paradigm.

items.title: From Foundation to Frontier: Re-Examining Bloom’s Taxonomy Across the Four Levels of Education in ICT and Generative AI Era
items.abstract: Bloom’s Taxonomy remains one of the most enduring pedagogical frameworks in global education, offering a structured hierarchy of cognitive processes from Remembering to Creating. In the age of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and generative artificial intelligence (AI), its relevance has been both reinforced and problematised. This article argues that the effectiveness of Bloom’s Taxonomy is not uniform across the four levels of education—Primary, Secondary, Higher Secondary, and Tertiary—but rather varies in emphasis and application according to students’ cognitive development, curricular demands, and the affordances of digital tools. Drawing on contemporary scholarship and the Bangladeshi educational context, the article proposes a differentiated model of Bloom’s application, where lower-order cognitive skills (LOCS) dominate early schooling while higher-order cognitive skills (HOCS) become progressively central. It further contends that Bloom’s Taxonomy, while necessary, is insufficient in the AI era unless complemented by digital literacy, AI literacy, ethical reasoning, and process-oriented assessment. The article concludes with implications for curriculum design, teacher development, and assessment reform.

items.title: From Molecules to Medicines
items.abstract: Drug discovery takes a long time, usually 10 to 15 years. It also costs more than USD 2 billion for each approved drug, with clinical failure rates close to 90%. Traditional linear processes find it hard to tackle complicated issues like chronic diseases, antimicrobial resistance, and new health threats. Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are goal-directed structures that combine large language models, reinforcement learning, and multi-agent setups. They allow for fully automated, closed-loop drug discovery. These AI systems can identify targets, create and improve molecules, design and run experiments in robotic labs, and continuously change strategies based on real-time feedback. Even with their ability to cut down on time, costs, and failure rates, challenges still exist related to understanding, data bias, ethics, and regulatory oversight.

items.title: From Search to Co-Planning: How Vietnamese Independent Travelers Use, Verify, And Act on Generative Ai Recommendations
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how travelers search for information and plan trips, yet much of the existing research still focuses on technology adoption, trust, or continuance intentions rather than on the process through which an AI recommendation is checked and translated into an actual decision. This study explores how Vietnamese independent travelers use GenAI in trip planning, how they evaluate and verify AI outputs, and how they decide whether to accept, modify, or reject those recommendations. An exploratory qualitative design was employed, involving 28 participants who had used GenAI to plan a specific independent trip. Data were collected through semi-structured in-depth interviews and analyzed using the Gioia methodology. The findings suggest that GenAI is shifting from a search tool toward a co-planning partner; however, its outputs are rarely received entirely passively. Travelers engage in selective verification depending on perceived risk, information volatility, and decision reversibility, while calibrating their trust according to the task and prior experience. Four ways of integrating AI recommendations into travel decisions were identified: direct acceptance, acceptance after verification, modified acceptance, and rejection. The study therefore proposes the concept of “verified co-planning” and develops a process model in which verification and trust calibration connect AI recommendations with action. These findings extend process-based understanding of GenAI in tourism and clarify how travelers preserve agency as AI becomes more deeply embedded in travel planning.

items.title: From Segmentation to Simulation: Large Language Model Agents as Synthetic Consumers — Promise and Validity Risks for Marketing Strategy
items.abstract: Marketing strategy has always run on representations of the consumer: segments, personas, focus-group transcripts, survey panels. Large language models (LLMs) introduce a new representation — synthetic consumers: prompted model agents that answer surveys, react to concepts, simulate word of mouth and role-play purchase decisions at negligible marginal cost and near-zero elapsed time. Vendors now market such simulations as substitutes for early-stage consumer research, and strategy teams are using them to pre-test positioning, pricing framings and creative concepts before spending on human respondents. This conceptual paper examines what synthetic consumers can and cannot legitimately do for marketing strategy. We distinguish four uses — exploration, pre-testing, augmentation of human samples, and substitution — and argue that validity risk rises sharply across them. Drawing on the automation–augmentation paradox and on the psychometric requirements of construct validity, we identify five validity threats specific to LLM respondents: training-data echo, persona stereotyping, sycophantic and demand-characteristic responses, temporal freezing, and the absence of stakes. We propose a validation protocol — benchmark-against-humans, holdout concepts, adversarial prompting, and disclosure — under which synthetic consumers can be used defensibly in strategy work, and three propositions for empirical research. The paper's central claim is deliberately narrow: synthetic consumers are a powerful instrument for generating and screening hypotheses about consumers, and a dangerous instrument for confirming them.

items.title: From Thought to Thwaction: Where Thoughts Come From, How They Become Action, and What They Are Worth
items.abstract: Research on human thinking explains how thoughts arise and how decisions are made, but rarely asks how a thought becomes an action, how the way thinking begins can be trained, and what a thought is worth. This conceptual paper answers these questions from Kirdomicism, an action-centric philosophy. It introduces the thwaction, a thorough thought carried by will into effective action, with accountability for its result, summarised in the conceptual equation Thinking × Action = Avalrem, where Avalrem is the unit of action value. The paper argues that a decision is not the end of thinking but the middle of an action; that self-force, willpower developed into habit, carries thought into action; that thoughts arise from a life setting described by the Buddhist Five Aggregates, with each first thought unpredictable but the mind’s tendencies trainable through a tool-free daily thwaction cycle; and that a thought has no value until it becomes action. The paper engages research on the intention–behaviour gap, implementation intentions, habit, spontaneous thought, prospection, cognitive offloading to artificial intelligence and the economics of ideas, including proposals to pay people for their data. It offers 23 propositions classified as definitional, explanatory or normative, two new measures (the thwaction count and the thwaction rate), and a research agenda of five studies.

items.title: From Waste to Wealth: Integrating Biological Systems and Molecular Intelligence for Lignin Valorization
items.abstract: Lignin is an abundant and renewable aromatic polymer, but its structural heterogeneity hinders its efficient bioconversion. Unlike previous reviews that focused on isolated topics such as single enzymes, pathway engineering, or specific bioproducts, this paper comprehensively reviews the latest advances in the structural characteristics, microbial degradation mechanisms, and bioconversion of lignin. Particular emphasis is placed on the catalytic mechanisms of key lignin-degrading enzymes, including laccase, lignin peroxidase (LiP), and manganese peroxidase (MnP), as well as the applications of fungi, bacteria, and synthetic microbial consortia in lignin bioconversion. Metabolic pathways that channel heterogeneous lignin-derived aromatics into central carbon metabolism through sequential catalytic reactions are also covered. Furthermore, we evaluate the emerging applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning in enzyme design and bioprocess control. Finally, techno-economic and life-cycle considerations are integrated to guide large-scale deployment. This review provides in-depth insights into the cross-scale translation from laboratory biocatalysis to industrial biorefineries.

items.title: From Weakly Supervised Segmentation to Diagnostic Decisions: An Annotation-Economics Review for Medical Imaging
items.abstract: Accurate medical image segmentation and the diagnostic decisions it supports are increasingly constrained by the cost of supervision: dense voxel-level annotation by expert clinicians remains slow, expensive, and difficult to scale, leaving many anatomies, pathologies, and modalities sparsely labeled. A large literature therefore relaxes the demand for full masks, yet existing surveys often catalog broad forms of limited supervision without directly comparing the practical trade-off between label granularity, annotation burden, and segmentation quality. This review focuses on weakly and coarsely labeled settings (image-level tags, points/clicks, bounding boxes, scribbles, and coarse masks, together with gaze or partial annotations as separate, protocol-dependent forms of supervision) and organizes them through an annotation-economics perspective that considers per-case annotation cost, required expertise, scalability, and the reported performance gap relative to full supervision. The evidence suggests that box and scribble supervision can provide favorable cost–performance trade-offs in several medical segmentation studies, although the reported metrics and datasets are heterogeneous and should not be interpreted as a unified quantitative frontier. We next examine the foundation-model turn, namely the Segment Anything Model and its medical derivatives, and argue that promptable models re-encode rather than eliminate human supervision, moving part of the effort from offline labeling to inference-time interaction. Finally, we extend the analysis beyond Dice to ask whether weakly produced masks support downstream clinical tasks: aggregate measurements may be relatively tolerant of moderate boundary error, whereas texture and high-order radiomic features can be substantially more sensitive. We close by identifying benchmark fragmentation, annotation variability, and the still-limited evidence connecting weak segmentation to clinical outcomes as open problems and propose a unified “weak label → task” benchmark for future evaluation.
